name: Zane Lopez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Zane, and thanks for making time. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government, and we don't sell or campaign for anything. Everything you say is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. This is a made-up study built around people like you, and there are no right answers. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: A normal week is a mix of lectures and building things. Monday and Tuesday are heavy theory, then I spend Wednesday to Friday in the game lab, where our small team is making a puzzle game about a lighthouse keeper. I use AI tools all day: for code suggestions, for art placeholders, for explaining errors. Weekends I play five-a-side football with some guys from my corridor, and I stream a bit of my coding on a tiny channel with eleven viewers.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Why computer science, and why games?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My mum owns a dental clinic and my dad's a sound engineer, so I grew up between machines and people who like them. I got top grades, and my parents pay for everything, so no debt. I like making things fast and seeing if they work. That's why I use the tools: they let me try five versions in the time I'd have made one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first of five pictures. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, but nicely. The tools are great, and I use them every day, but they're an assistant, not a revolution. I'd tell my friends that doesn't make them bad, it makes them tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be a little let down. Part of why I chose this course is to be in the middle of something big. But I'd be fine: I'd still be building games, and my parents' work wouldn't change. A calmer world is easier on my family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep making games and push to publish one on a small store before the end of the year. I'd use the AI tools for the dull parts and keep the creative parts mine. I'd also apply for a summer job at a studio, ideally a small one where you do everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels pleasant, a bit like a long, flat Sunday afternoon.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you actually want more change, even if it were risky?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. I like risk when it's mine. I'd like some change in what's possible, like making a game alone that used to need ten people. But I don't want my mum's clinic or my dad's work to be at risk for my excitement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your first published game need to succeed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A hook you can describe in one sentence, and polish. I'd find ten friends to test it, listen to what annoys them, and fix that. I'd also be fine if only a few hundred people play it. The point is to ship something.

say: I'd say the tools are great but they're an **assistant**, not a revolution.
I'd tell friends that doesn't make them **bad**, it makes them tools.
think: I'm a little **let down**, because I wanted to be in the middle of something big.
A calmer world is easier on my **family**.
do: Publish a small **game** on a store before year end.
Use AI for the **dull** parts and keep creative work mine.
Apply for a summer job at a small **studio**.
feel: Pleasant, like a long, **flat** Sunday afternoon.
S0.quote: I don't want my mum's clinic or my dad's work to be at risk for my excitement.
fieldNote: Thrill-seeker by nature, yet careful with **other** people's livelihoods.
Uses AI for dull work and keeps the creative decisions for himself.
Calm is justified by money, skills and a family whose work is stable.

steps.text: Ship a small puzzle game on a game store this year
Use AI tools for repetitive code and keep design personal
Apply for a summer job at a small studio

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the next picture. It's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, finally. It's real, so let's learn it properly. I'd tell my course mates that the people who learn to work with it will be fine, and the ones who wait will have a harder time. I'd say it in a friendly way, though, not a smug one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be excited and a bit nervous. Coding is exactly what the card says goes first, so entry-level roles would be fewer. But I already work with these tools all day, and I'd rather be a person who can run a team of them than a person who competes with them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go for projects that show I can ship whole things alone: games, tools, small apps. I'd put them online, enter some game jams, and ask studios for short paid contracts. I'd also learn basics of business and design, so I'm not just a coder, since coding becomes cheaper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like surfing. Scary if you think about the size of the wave, fun if you're on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to a classmate who doesn't like using AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say try it for a week with one rule: you have to explain every line it writes. That way you still learn. I know people who think using it is cheating, and I'd listen, but I'd say it's like using a calculator when the maths is the point, and sometimes it isn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about this picture that really worries you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jobs for people who don't have the same head start. I'm lucky: I learned the tools early and my family can pay while I try things. For a person without that, a year of fewer hires would hit hard, and I'd feel that without being able to fix it.

say: I'd say it's real, so let's **learn** it properly.
I'd tell classmates the ones who wait will have a **harder** time, said kindly.
think: I'm **excited** and a bit nervous, since coding goes first.
I'd rather run a team of tools than **compete** with them.
do: Ship whole **projects** and enter game jams.
Learn **business** and design basics so I'm more than a coder.
feel: Like **surfing**: scary if you think about the wave, fun if you're on it.
S1.quote: I'd rather be a person who can run a team of them than a person who competes with them.
fieldNote: Treats the tools as a **crew** to manage; his confidence comes from daily practice.
Worries about people without his head start and family money.
Practical about shipping: jams, contracts, and business skills beyond code.

steps.text: Enter two game jams this term and publish the results
Ask small studios for short paid contracts
Take business and design modules to widen skills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the next picture. It's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say wow, okay, and then I'd say we need to talk properly about what comes next. Two years is crazy. I'd say tools like this change the world, and people need help, not slogans. I'd want to hear every honest plan from governments and from the companies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel both excited and scared. If thinking AI can do almost anything I can, my degree changes meaning. But the hands-on world lasts until around 2031, and I'm fast at picking things up. I'd be more worried for my mum's clinic suppliers, my dad's studio clients, and my friends who didn't use the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd test every tool I could, build a small business that uses them, and ask my parents if they'd back me with a modest sum. I'd start looking for a way to combine games with something physical, like VR or installations, because those are tied to real spaces. And I'd save everything I earn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels huge and weirdly personal, like when the lights go out in a stadium before the show starts. I don't know if the show will be good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd start a business. Is that bravery or panic?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe both. I'd say it's a way of staying in control. If I'm going to have to work in a world where machines are cheap, I'd rather be the one who owns some of them than the one waiting to be hired.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my mum that a clinic is a good place to be, because patients still want a person with a drill. I'd tell my dad that sound design might shift fast and he should try the tools before his clients tell him to. I'd be honest that I'm not sure.

say: I'd say we need to talk about what comes next, with **honest** plans from governments and firms.
I'd say people need **help**, not slogans.
think: I'd feel **excited** and scared; my degree changes meaning.
I'd worry for **friends** who didn't use the tools.
do: Test every **tool** and build a small business using them.
Combine games with something **physical**, like VR installations.

feel: Like the lights going out in a **stadium** before the show starts.
S2.quote: I'd rather be the one who owns some of them than the one waiting to be hired.
fieldNote: Answers fear with **ownership**: build a business that uses the machines.
His worries are for friends, his father's sound clients and others, not for himself.
Uneasy rather than anxious because his family's income stays stable in this picture.

steps.text: Test every new tool and build a small business around them
Prototype a VR game for physical venues
Save all earnings and ask parents for modest backing
Teach his dad the new sound tools before clients ask

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the next picture. It's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is exciting and sensible. We have time to build things, so let's build things. I'd say schools should teach people to work with AI from age ten, and employers should train people instead of just replacing them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel pretty good. I'd graduate in three years with experience in AI tools, a few shipped projects and maybe a small company. The robots come around 2034, so there's a window. I'd be a bit nervous about whether I'm kidding myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, run a small studio with two or three friends from my course, and take on freelance jobs. I'd keep saving. I'd also learn something that makes me useful in the real world, maybe electronics, because hands-on skills stay valued longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like a game with a clear timer. Stressful, but fun to play.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How is it different from the two-year picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years, I'd be improvising. With five, I can plan a path. I could finish my degree, build up some savings and test a business in my spare time. The extra three years are what turn it from a stampede into a track.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Are you kidding yourself at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Possibly. I tend to assume I'll land on my feet, because I always have. It's easy to be confident when your family can pay for the landing. I try to remember that when I give advice to others.

I'd say schools should teach AI from age ten and employers should **train** people.

I'm a bit nervous about **kidding** myself.

S3.quote: The extra three years are what turn it from a stampede into a track.
fieldNote: Time turns his **improvising** into a plan; he sees the difference between the two- and five-year cases.
Admits his confidence rests on family money, which keeps him honest.

steps.text: Form a small studio with two friends from the course
Take freelance jobs and save most of the income
Learn basic electronics in evening workshops

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the next picture. It's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, so no panic. I'd say we should keep the good parts and fix the bad ones, and I'd say my generation will probably get to build whatever comes next.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel excited. Ten years takes me through the degree and a few years of working, probably founding something. The date might shift, and I'd be fine with that. I'd keep an eye on whether the world gets fairer or more unequal, which depends on choices people make now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on: finish the degree, build a portfolio, and work at a studio or start my own. I'd also learn how money works, so I can invest sensibly. And I'd keep doing the football and streaming, since a long runway means you can still have a life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels bright, a bit like looking at a travel brochure. Lovely, but I know the weather is never exactly as pictured.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the extra years that you couldn't do with fewer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably try one idea that fails. Something I'd not risk if I only had two years. A failed project costs less when you have a decade, and you learn more from it than from a safe plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to a friend who thinks this is all too fast?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say take a breath, and pick one thing to learn this year. You don't need to master everything. And talk to someone older, because they've seen a few big changes and they usually have something calm to say.

I'd say my generation will probably get to **build** what comes next.
think: I'd feel **excited**: degree, a few working years, probably founding something.
Fairness depends on **choices** people make now.

Learn how **money** works so I can invest sensibly.
feel: Bright, like a travel **brochure**, though the weather is never as pictured.

fieldNote: The long **runway** invites him to take a risk he would avoid with two years.
Advice to a worried friend is to learn one thing this year and talk to older people.
Optimistic, with a self-aware note that fairness depends on choices.

steps.text: Try one risky game idea and accept that it may fail
Learn basic investing and start a small share account
Build a portfolio of three shipped projects

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because there'd be no time for people without my head start. What would help is free access to the tools and training for everybody, and some kind of income cushion while things settle.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I know I sound optimistic, and I want that to be fair. Liking change is easy when you have a safety net. I'd want everyone to have one.

headlineQuote: Liking change is easy when you have a safety net. I'd want everyone to have one.
portrait: Zane is an 18-year-old **computer science** student who makes games and uses AI tools all day.
He is centrist and adaptive: he tries things early, builds small businesses in his head, and likes risk when it's his.
His parents, a dentist and a sound engineer, pay for everything, and he knows that **money** shapes his confidence.
He mostly stays calm, turning only **uneasy** in the two-year picture, where he would start a business.
He worries about friends without his head start and wants fair access to tools and training.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** picture, because people without his head start would have no time.
whatWouldHelp: Free access to the tools and **training** for everyone, plus an income cushion.
